In brief

Doffing his dressing gown, Mulligan likens himself to the Savior humiliated by Roman soldiers prior to being nailed to a cross and hung up to die: "Mulligan is stripped of his garments." In Scylla and Charybdis Stephen follows suit, reciting for Mulligan's benefit (he has just been thinking of the "Brood of mockers: Photius, pseudomalachi, Johann Most") the fact that Jesus, "stripped and whipped, was nailed like bat to barndoor." This event from Christ's passion is one of fourteen stages in the Catholic devotional practice called the Stations of the Cross. Another such "station" is alluded to in Circe.

At more length

The Via Crucis is a numbered series of narrative images through which western Christian churches commemorate Christ’s journey down the Via Dolorosa on his way to being crucified at Calvary. Practitioners proceed from one image to the next, contemplating Christ's sufferings and spiritually aligning themselves with him through meditations and prayers. The tenth of the fourteen stations, "Jesus is stripped of his clothes," echoes Matthew's gospel: “And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe” (27:28). Mulligan flippantly makes light of this searing scene.

His real-life model, Oliver Gogarty, was known for doing the same thing. When Stephen confronts his dead mother in Circe Joyce has Mulligan say, "Mulligan meets the afflicted mother," reenacting something that Gogarty was famous for saying about his own mother when he trudged up her front stairs reciting the Stations of the Cross.

John Hunt 2017
